tagline: An early auto-touring road crosses mountains and follows five rivers
intro: The Mohawk Trail climbs out of North Adams on a steep, curving road toward the Hoosac Range, then descends eastward beside the Cold River to the Deerfield. Forest, river crossings and historic towns define the 69-mile National Scenic Byway. Western Massachusetts Scenic Byways highlights its art museums, early tourist destinations and five rivers, from the Hoosic to the Millers.

The corridor began as a Native American trading route across the Hoosac Range. European settlers later altered the route for horses and carts; growing automobile use brought another transformation. The scenic road officially opened on October 22, 1914. Today’s Routes 2 and 2A follow much of the older trail. Along the Cold River, the historic footpath route lay north of the water; the modern road follows the south bank. River-powered mills helped these towns grow during the nineteenth century; the early auto route later brought souvenir shops, tourist cottages and restaurants.

Travel east from Williamstown through North Adams, climb past the hairpin turn to Whitcomb Summit, and descend toward Charlemont. Follow the Deerfield toward Shelburne Falls and its former trolley bridge, now a flower garden. Beyond Greenfield, the French King Bridge crosses the Connecticut; farther east the Millers River accompanies the route through Erving toward Orange and Athol.

moments.title: The Hairpin Turn
moments.text: On the western side of Whitcomb Summit, the hairpin turn’s lookout faces North Adams and the Taconic Mountains. The road climbs steeply from the city toward the West Summit. North Adams occupies the Hoosic River valley, where the meeting of two river branches supplied water power for early manufacturing. Farther east, the mountain crossing takes a different line: from Whitcomb Summit, the highway descends the Hoosac Range along the Cold River to the Deerfield. The scenic road opened in 1914, among the country’s early routes built for auto touring through this landscape.
moments.notice: North Adams and the Taconic Mountains are visible from the hairpin lookout.

moments.title: Bridge of Flowers
moments.text: A water main helped save the trolley bridge that became Shelburne Falls’ flower garden. The garden occupies a seasonal footbridge connecting Shelburne and Buckland. Built in 1908 for the Shelburne Falls and Colrain Street Railway, it connected rail freight with Colrain. The neighboring Iron Bridge had a twenty-ton weight limit. As trucks gained freight business, the railway went bankrupt in 1927. Antoinette Burnham proposed a garden, and local women’s clubs raised money for the transformation. Eighty loads of loam arrived in 1929. Beneath the flowers, soil reaches two and a half feet deep over the arches and nine feet at the piers.

moments.title: French King Bridge
moments.text: The French King Bridge carries Route 2 across the Connecticut River between Gill and Erving. Its opening in 1932 changed the highway’s course: Route 2 moved from the older crossing through Turners Falls to French King Highway. The American Institute of Steel Construction awarded it the title “Most Beautiful Steel Bridge” for 1932, the year it opened to traffic. The bridge was rebuilt in 1992 and refurbished in 2008–2010. Nine-foot steel barriers were added on both sides in 2023. Its name comes from French King Rock, visible in the middle of the river.
